```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(DesignComplexSurvival)
```

DesignComplexSurvival computes the operating characteristics of two-group
time-to-event trials analysed with the log-rank test, without patient-level
simulation. Each group follows a four-state model (progression-free,
progressed, switched, dead) with piecewise constant intensities. This
vignette shows a single endpoint with a delayed treatment effect, then
overall survival (OS) with treatment switching after progression, and
finally progression-free survival (PFS) and OS tested together.

## A delayed treatment effect

The control group has exponential survival with a median of 12 months. In
the treatment group the hazard ratio is 1 for the first 6 months and 0.65
afterwards. Patients are enrolled at 10 per month for 3 months and at 30 per
month afterwards, and the dropout hazard is 0.003 per month in both groups.

```{r delayed-scenario}
lam <- log(2) / 12
ctl <- ms_model(death = lam, dropout = 0.003)
trt <- ms_model(time = c(0, 6), death = c(lam, 0.65 * lam), dropout = 0.003)
acc <- ms_accrual(time = c(0, 3), rate = c(10, 30))
scn <- ms_scenario(ctl, trt, allocation = 1, accrual = acc)
ev <- ms_events(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = c(12, 24, 36))
ev[, c("time", "enrolled", "events_control", "events_treatment", "events")]
```

With 700 patients, `r round(ev$events[3])` events are expected by month 36.

The design has interim analyses at 50 and 75 percent of the events, an
efficacy bound of O'Brien-Fleming type and a non-binding futility bound by
beta spending. `ms_size()` finds the number of events for a power of 90
percent.

```{r delayed-size}
looks <- ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.5, 0.75, 1))
test <- ms_test(futility = "beta", sf_fut = "HSD", param_fut = -2)
des <- ms_size(scn, looks = looks, test = test, power = 0.9,
               solve_for = "events", n = 700)
des
```

The accrual ends at month `r round(des$accrual_duration, 1)`. The final
analysis needs `r des$events` events and takes place at month
`r round(des$study_duration, 1)`. The type I error is
`r signif(des$type1[["nonbinding"]], 3)` when the futility bounds are
ignored.

The mean of the standardized statistic can be computed directly from the
hazards (default) or with the Schoenfeld approximation, which uses the
event-weighted average of the log hazard ratio.

```{r delayed-mean}
t_fin <- des$study_duration
rbind(direct = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin)$z_mean,
      schoenfeld = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin, mean = "schoenfeld")$z_mean)
```

## Overall survival with switching after progression

In the control group the hazard of progression is 0.10 per month in the
first 4 months and 0.08 afterwards. At progression, 30 percent of the
patients switch to the experimental treatment; the others may switch later
with a hazard of 0.04 per month. After progression the hazard of death is
0.06 without switch and 0.035 after a switch. The treatment group has a
lower hazard of progression and no switching.

```{r switch-models}
ctl_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   switch_prob = 0.3, death_prog = 0.06, switch_rate = 0.04,
                   death_switch = 0.035, dropout = 0.003)
trt_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.06, 0.05), death = 0.008,
                   death_prog = 0.055, dropout = 0.003)
ms_prob(ctl_sw, time = c(6, 12, 24))
```

The post-progression intensities are measured from the time of progression
(`clock = "reset"`, the default). OS and progression-free survival (PFS) of
the control group at 12 months are
`r round(ms_surv(ctl_sw, 12, "os")$surv, 3)` and
`r round(ms_surv(ctl_sw, 12, "pfs")$surv, 3)`.

```{r switch-power}
scn_sw <- ms_scenario(ctl_sw, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
pw <- ms_power(scn_sw, n = 500, looks = ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.6, 1)),
               test = ms_test(), events = 300)
pw
```

With 300 OS events the power is `r round(pw$power, 3)`. Switching to the
experimental treatment in the control group moves the hazard ratio for OS
towards 1. For comparison, the same design without switching (all switching
intensities set to zero) has the power

```{r switch-none}
ctl_ns <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   death_prog = 0.06, dropout = 0.003)
scn_ns <- ms_scenario(ctl_ns, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
pw_ns <- ms_power(scn_ns, n = 500, looks = ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.6, 1)),
                  test = ms_test(), events = 300)
pw_ns$power
```

## PFS and OS tested together

Both groups follow the model of Fleischer et al. (2009): the times to
progression and to death are exponential and the hazard of death does not
change at progression, so that PFS and OS are exponential. The medians of
PFS and OS are 4 and 12 months in the control group and 6 and 16 months in
the treatment group, and patients are enrolled at 25 per month.

PFS is tested at 300 PFS events, where OS is also tested, and OS is tested
again at 220 OS events. With the fixed-sequence procedure, both hypotheses
are tested at level 0.025 and OS is tested only after PFS has been rejected
(procedure (b) of Glimm et al. 2010). Each endpoint has its own efficacy
bounds of O'Brien-Fleming type.

```{r two-design}
fl <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                  ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 16),
                  accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
lk2 <- ms_looks(c("pfs", "os"), fraction = c(1, 1),
                test = list(c("pfs", "os"), "os"))
fs <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
               events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220))
fs
```

The power is `r round(fs$power[["pfs"]], 3)` for PFS and
`r round(fs$power[["os"]], 3)` for OS, and both hypotheses are rejected
with probability `r round(fs$power[["both"]], 3)`. The final OS analysis
takes place at month `r round(fs$study_duration, 1)`.

The Bonferroni procedure tests PFS at level 0.02 and OS at level 0.005,
whatever happens to the other hypothesis.

```{r two-bonferroni}
bf <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "bonferroni",
                              weights = c(0.8, 0.2)),
               events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220))
rbind(fixed_sequence = fs$power, bonferroni = bf$power)
```

The familywise error rate is computed under the global null hypothesis,
where the correlation between the PFS and OS statistics is that of Danzer
et al. (2025). A partial null hypothesis, in which OS is the same in both
groups but PFS is not, can be given through `null_scenarios`:

```{r two-fwer}
os_null <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                       ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 12),
                       accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
         test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
         events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220), null_scenarios = list(os = os_null))$fwer
```

## Choice of the covariance

The argument `variance` of `ms_test()` (and of `lr_moments()` and
`lr_cov()`) chooses the covariance of the standardized statistics. By
default (`"null"`) the statistics of one endpoint have unit variances and
the correlations of independent increments. With `"alternative"`, the
variance and covariance of the score under the alternative hypothesis (Luo
et al. 2019) are used instead. With `"studentized"`, the covariance is the
asymptotic covariance of the statistic that is computed in practice,
standardized by the estimated variance and, for event-driven analyses,
taken at a random analysis time.

```{r alt-var}
mo <- lapply(c(alternative = "alternative", studentized = "studentized"),
             function(v) lr_moments(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = c(24, t_fin),
                                    variance = v))
sapply(mo, function(m) m$z_var)
```

Here the largest difference of the variances from 1 is
`r signif(max(abs(mo$alternative$z_var - 1)), 2)` with `"alternative"` and
`r signif(max(abs(mo$studentized$z_var - 1)), 2)` with `"studentized"`.
The choice affects the power and the futility bounds by beta spending, but
not the efficacy bounds or the non-binding type I error. In the simulations
of `inst/validation/` with PFS and OS tested together, `"studentized"`
agreed best with the simulated standard deviations and correlations of the
statistics, and the powers with `"null"` and `"studentized"` agreed with
the simulated powers within the Monte Carlo error.

## References

Danzer MF, Rufibach K, Beyersmann J, Schmidt R (2025). Exhausting the type I
error level in event-driven group-sequential designs with a closed testing
procedure for progression-free and overall survival. arXiv:2512.08658.

Fleischer F, Gaschler-Markefski B, Bluhmki E (2009). A statistical model for
the dependence between progression-free survival and overall survival.
Statistics in Medicine 28:2669-2686.

Glimm E, Maurer W, Bretz F (2010). Hierarchical testing of multiple
endpoints in group-sequential trials. Statistics in Medicine 29:219-228.

Luo X, Mao X, Chen X, Qiu J, Bai S, Quan H (2019). Design and monitoring of
survival trials in complex scenarios. Statistics in Medicine 38:192-209.
